name: Paediatric trigger thumb
aliases: stenosing tenosynovitis of the thumb in children

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Presents as a fixed or catching flexion of the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, usually noticed in toddlers rather than at birth, so it is frequently not truly congenital
A palpable nodule (Notta's node) is felt at the level of the A1 pulley over the volar aspect of the metacarpophalangeal region, representing thickening of the flexor pollicis longus tendon
The underlying problem is a size mismatch or stenosis between the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the A1 pulley, restricting smooth tendon gliding
Unlike in adults, painful triggering is uncommon; the usual presentation is a thumb held flexed at the interphalangeal joint, sometimes discovered when the child cannot straighten it
It is often bilateral, so both thumbs should be examined; the differential includes a congenital clasped thumb and a thumb-in-palm deformity
Many cases resolve spontaneously, particularly in the youngest children, so a period of observation with or without stretching and splinting is reasonable
Persistent fixed deformity is treated by surgical release of the A1 pulley, which is highly effective and durable
reference.pathophysiology: The condition arises from a mismatch between the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the mouth of the A1 pulley at the base of the thumb. Thickening of the tendon, forming the palpable Notta's node, together with relative narrowing of the pulley, impedes smooth gliding so that the thumb catches or becomes locked in flexion at the interphalangeal joint. Because the deformity is commonly absent at birth and only appears later in infancy or early childhood, it is regarded as a developmental or acquired stenosing tenosynovitis rather than a truly congenital anomaly.
additionalDifferentials: Thumb-in-palm deformity, for example in cerebral palsy or spasticity
Trigger finger affecting the other digits
A skeletal anomaly limiting interphalangeal joint extension
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis by palpation of Notta's node and demonstration of fixed interphalangeal flexion or triggering
Examination of both thumbs given frequent bilaterality, and of the other digits
Assessment for associated neurological or arthrogrypotic conditions when the presentation is atypical
Radiographs only if a bony abnormality or an alternative diagnosis is suspected
Serial documentation of passive and active interphalangeal extension to track spontaneous resolution
redFlags: A thumb that cannot be passively extended, suggesting a fixed contracture rather than simple triggering
Atypical features suggesting a neurological or syndromic cause
Multiple-digit involvement raising suspicion of a metabolic storage disorder (such as a mucopolysaccharidosis)
reference.prognosis: A substantial proportion resolve spontaneously, especially when identified in infancy; for thumbs that remain fixed, release of the A1 pulley gives reliable and lasting correction with a low complication rate.
pitfalls: Assuming the condition is present from birth and labelling it congenital, when it usually appears later
Confusing it with a congenital clasped thumb, which is an extensor problem
Operating too early, before allowing a reasonable chance of spontaneous resolution
Injuring the digital nerves, which lie close to the A1 pulley, during release
